item.title: Age-dependent structural evolution of a functional amyloid contributes to memory impairment in Drosophila.
item.author: Ou S, Guillen-Poza PA, Ng KK, Xu L, Cheng BY, Yi Y, Ho LY, Franco-Fernández A, Khaki PSS, Mukhi M, Cheung KC, Sharma R, Oroz J, Hirano Y, Hervas R.
item.description:
Cryogenic electron microscopy has revealed endpoint structures of ex vivo amyloid filaments, but how amyloids assemble and evolve in living organisms-and how these transitions affect physiology-remains poorly understood. Here, we map the age-dependent structural landscape of Orb2 amyloid, a synaptic translation regulator required for long-term memory, across the adult lifespan of Drosophila melanogaster. By determining multiple Orb2 amyloid structures, we uncover a dynamic, age-linked progression of amyloid states. Translation-promoting assemblies predominate early in life, whereas aging shifts the Orb2 amyloid ensemble toward structurally distinct, destabilization-resistant assemblies with reduced translational activity, coinciding with memory impairment. item.title: Genetic coupling of floral rewards and signals underlies pollinator attraction.
item.author: Tan FQ, Slavkovic F, Zhang M, Adam G, Troadec C, Jiang ZH, Verdenaud M, Shirazi Parsa H, Cuzzi D, Liu X, Li X, Devani RS, Yan Y, Chen Q, Huang Y, Morison N, Zhang S, Marcel F, Gilard F, Gakiere B, Latrasse D, Benhamed M, Carcaud J, Sandoz JC, Vaissiere B, Boualem A, Dogimont C, Bendahmane A.
item.description:
Animal pollinators underpin biodiversity and global agriculture, yet the molecular mechanisms that coordinate floral rewards and signals to attract pollinators remain poorly understood. Through phenotyping melon genetic diversity, we identified nectarless1 (nls1), encoding the YABBY-family transcription factor YABBY5 (YAB5), as a central integrator of pollinator-attracting traits. YAB5 interacts with CRABS CLAW (CRC) during nectary initiation to specify nectary identity by repressing alternative floral organ fates. As flowers mature, YAB5 directly activates 4-α-glucanotransferase 2 (DPE2) to promote starch remobilization required for nectar secretion and promotes petal growth and flower opening. item.title: Innate sensor responses set a supra-unitary threshold for viral replication.
item.author: Mukai K, Jia D, Panigrahi M, Tayman T, Brogden G, Chen YH, Haque N, Arora G, Mutterperl JE, Poe I, Zhang C, Islam Z, Holewinski R, Andresson T, Wu D, Piszczek G, Marcotrigiano J, Hogg JR, De Ravin SS, Malik NS, Nath A, Viktorova E, Zimina A, Belov GA, Bayyurt-Kocabaş B, Altan-Bonnet G, Altan-Bonnet N.
item.description:
Cells resist viral infection by triggering rapid and sensitive innate immune responses, initiated by cytoplasmic viral sensor proteins (CyVSP), retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I), melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA-5), and protein kinase R (PKR). item.title: Multimodal spatial transcriptomics redefines cortical pathology in Huntington's disease.
item.author: Vazquez-Sanchez S, Arnold-Garcia O, Chillon-Marinas C, Maimon R, Cui J, McNair K, Dai Y, Jimenez NL, Child DD, Thompson LM, Lopez-Erauskin J, Bintu B, Cleveland DW.
item.description:
Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene (HTT), yet how somatic repeat instability and HTT inclusions relate to selective cell loss in the human brain remains unclear. We have developed a multimodal spatial transcriptomics approach that enables the definition of transcriptional programs with subcellular resolution, somatic CAG repeat lengths, and eight other pathology markers, including HTT inclusions, in every cell of intact brain sections. Imaging 428,173 cells in the control and HD cortex revealed the selective vulnerability of layer 5-6 (L5-6) near-projecting (NP) neurons and L6b deep-layer excitatory neurons, which undergo a >50% loss that is closely linked to large somatic repeat expansions (>450 ± 55 CAGs). item.title: Somatic DNA-repeat expansions initiate distinct yet analogous changes in Huntington's disease cortical and striatal neurons.
item.author: Kashin S, Lee WS, McDonald TM, Morris K, Handsaker RE, Mello CJ, Spina L, Reed NM, de Rivera H, Jana SH, Hogan M, Berretta S, McCarroll SA.
item.description:
Huntington's disease (HD) affects the neocortex and striatum with different timing, severity, and gene-expression changes. These pathologies have long been proposed to involve different pathogenic mechanisms, with one brain area's degeneration leading to the other's. Striatal neurons degenerate in HD as their huntingtin (HTT) CAG-repeat tracts expand somatically beyond 150 CAGs. Here, we find that cortical pyramidal neurons in HD undergo biological changes analogous to those in striatal neurons-the same sequence of pathological phases, with toxicity also commencing at ∼150 CAGs but then changing their gene expression in distinct ways. Pyramidal neurons' precise molecular identities, rather than their areal or laminar locations, appeared to determine the extent of this somatic DNA-repeat expansion, which varied up to 20-fold among pyramidal neuron subtypes. item.title: Long-range actin-driven endosymbiont mobility in an animal-algal symbiosis.
item.author: Zhong G, Toullec G, Jouneau PH, Decelle J, Prakash M.
item.description:
In animal-microbe symbioses, established symbionts are often thought to be confined to a niche and to lose motile appendages such as flagella. Whether this loss implies immobility within the host remains poorly understood. We report long-range, host-driven symbiont mobility in a dinoflagellate-acoel worm symbiosis. Using long-term tracking, fluorescence, and electron microscopy, we find that hundreds of dinoflagellate symbionts (Amphidinium sp., 10-20 μm in size) travel across the body of an acoel worm host (Waminoa sp.) at around 1 μm/s while confined inside a network of ultra-thin (∼200 nm) host parenchymal cells. We show this mobility is driven by host actin machinery, with symbionts moving faster than comparable actin-based transport systems despite confinement. item.title: Deep sequencing of 3,367 maize genomes uncovers substantial contribution of rare variants to agronomic traits.
item.author: Huang L, Bian C, Xin B, Zhang X, Lu Q, Yue Y, Li Y, Zeng R, Liu X, Fan X, Wang T, Wang Y, Cao J, Zhang J, Wu J, Lin Z, Zhao J, Cheng W, Gao S, Chen Y, Lu Y, Yang J, Liu W, Chen Z, Sun H, Lu X, Xue J, Yang S, Liu Q, Chen J, Zhao H, Zhao H, Song W, Lai J.
item.description:
Rare variants are highly abundant, yet their genome-wide contributions to agronomic traits remain elusive in plants. Here, we performed deep whole-genome sequencing of 3,367 diverse elite maize inbred lines, uncovering 75.3 million variants, of which 79.2% were rare. Overall, we identified 411 independent association signals for 10 agronomic traits, including 359 attributable to globally rare variants, with rare variants showing effect sizes approximately 2.4 times those of common variants. Frequency-stratified genome-based restricted maximum likelihood (GREML) analyses indicated that rare variants captured a substantial proportion of phenotypic variance for traits under strong adaptive selection, consistent with the allele frequencies of trait-associated variants shifting from common in tropical to rare in temperate maize. item.title: In vivo genome-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Preclinical studies and first-in-human trial.
item.author: Li G, Han F, Wang C, Jin M, Lin J, Zhang H, Yan X, Wang X, Sun X, Yuan Y, Zhang S, Zhang S, Zhu J, Xu Y, Wang Y, Deng Y, Li F, Shi L, Luk A, Wang N, Yang H, Wang J.
item.description:
We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector. In humanized DMD mice, systemic administration achieved targeted genome editing, partial dystrophin restoration, and improved muscle function. In non-human primates, efficient on-target editing was achieved with no dose-limiting toxicity identified under the conditions tested. In an open-label, dose-escalation, first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06594094), post-treatment muscle biopsies provided early molecular evidence of hfCas12Max-mediated genome editing and detectable dystrophin expression in participants with DMD. item.title: Taurine lowers inflammaging by regulating the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages.
item.author: Guan C, Ryu S, Dong M, Zhu Y, Maeda R, Youm YH, Mohanty S, Kim HH, Orliaguet L, Dlugos T, Smith SR, Ravussin E, Onyuru J, Hoffman HM, Siebel S, Wang A, Wang Y, Kluger Y, Shaw AC, Kanneganti TD, LeBrasseur N, Sugiura Y, Dixit VD.
item.description:
Whether a decline in taurine drives aging is debated, and despite high millimolar intracellular concentrations, its function as a potential guardian of cytosolic homeostasis is unclear. Here, we show that aging increases circulating taurine concentrations in humans and mice. Further elevating taurine in aged mice enhances health span, engaging anti-inflammatory pathways previously linked to youthfulness, and reduces mortality from sepsis and inflammasome-mediated inflammation, suggesting an enantiostatic response. Mechanistically, diverse NLRP3-specific "danger signals" induce taurine efflux from macrophages as a proximal step to activate the inflammasome and the resultant pyroptosis. item.title: Perforin triggers iron-induced mitochondrial damage to drive ferroptosis and anti-tumor immunity.
item.author: Bell HN, Nair K, Tison K, Liao P, Lei H, El-Derany MO, Yisimayi A, Zhang H, Rebernick R, Wang W, Adachi Y, Castillo C, Das NK, An J, Sutton VR, Lin X, Lin H, Wang X, Li Y, Vatan L, Aboud A, Wei S, Gijon M, Goodwin S, Shah YM, Kryczek I, Trapani JA, Barroso M, Lieberman J, Zou W.
item.description:
Cytotoxic CD8 + T cells and natural killer cells are critical effectors of anti-tumor immunity. Cytotoxic lymphocytes eliminate tumor cells by releasing perforin (Prf1), a pore-forming protein that enables granzymes (Gzms) to enter target cells and trigger both caspase-dependent and -independent cell death. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized, Gzm-independent function of Prf1. We find that Prf1 directly induces tumoral ferroptosis, an iron- and lipid-dependent form of cell death. Mechanistically, Prf1-mediated pore formation drives endocytosis of the transferrin receptor, which increases cellular iron uptake. Prf1 promotes the formation of endosomal-mitochondrial contacts, which leads to mitochondrial iron accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and tumor cell ferroptosis.
